concept: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no duplicate characters.

solutions.label: Brute Force with Nested Loops
solutions.summary: Check every possible substring and verify each one has all unique characters.

solutions.label: Sliding Window with HashSet
solutions.summary: Use two pointers and a HashSet to expand and shrink a window of unique characters.

solutions.label: Optimized Sliding Window with HashMap
solutions.summary: Use a HashMap to store character positions and jump the left pointer directly past duplicates.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Input: 'abcabcbb'"] --> B["Substrings to consider"]
    B --> C["'abc' ✓ length 3"]
    B --> D["'bca' ✓ length 3"]
    B --> E["'abca' ✗ 'a' repeats"]
    C --> F["Answer: 3"]
    style A fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style F fill:#f87171,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's your problem. You're given a string, and you need to find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeating characters. For example, given the string a-b-c-a-b-c-b-b, the answer would be three, because a-b-c is the longest substring without duplicates.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So I need to find a contiguous part of the string where every character is unique, and return the maximum length. Can I ask a few clarifying questions? What characters can the string contain, and how long can it be?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The string consists of English letters, digits, and symbols. The length can be up to fifty thousand characters. It can also be empty.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What should I return for an empty string? And if every character is the same, like a-a-a-a, the answer would be one, correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, return zero for an empty string, and one if all characters are identical. You just return the length as an integer.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So to summarize: given a string, I find the longest contiguous substring with all unique characters and return its length. Let me start with a brute force approach.

sections.title: Brute Force with Nested Loops
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["String: 'p w w k e w'"] --> B["i=0: check 'p','pw','pww' ✗"]
    B --> C["i=1: check 'w','ww' ✗"]
    C --> D["i=2: check 'w','wk','wke','wkew' ✗"]
    D --> E["i=3: check 'k','ke','kew' ✓ len=3"]
    E --> F["Max length = 3"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style F fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is to check every possible substring. I use two nested loops: the outer loop picks a starting index, and the inner loop extends the end index. For each substring, I use a set to check if all characters are unique.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Take the string p-w-w-k-e-w. Starting from index zero, p is unique, p-w is unique, but p-w-w has a duplicate w, so I stop. I repeat this from every starting position and track the maximum length found.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The two loops give O of n-squared combinations, and checking each substring for uniqueness takes O of n in the worst case. So overall it's O of n-cubed, with O of n space for the set. That's quite slow for large inputs.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. Can you think of a way to avoid rechecking characters from scratch every time?

sections.title: Sliding Window with HashSet
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["String: 'p w w k e w'"] --> B["left=0, right=0: add 'p' → set={p}"]
    B --> C["right=1: add 'w' → set={p,w}"]
    C --> D["right=2: 'w' duplicate! remove 'p', left=1"]
    D --> E["still duplicate, remove 'w', left=2"]
    E --> F["right=2: add 'w' → set={w}"]
    F --> G["right=3: add 'k' → set={w,k}"]
    G --> H["right=4: add 'e' → set={w,k,e} max=3"]
    H --> I["right=5: 'w' dup, remove until clear"]
    I --> J["Result: 3"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style H fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style J fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Instead of checking every substring, I can use a sliding window. I maintain two pointers, left and right, and a HashSet. I move the right pointer forward, adding characters to the set. When I find a duplicate, I remove characters from the left until the duplicate is gone.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For p-w-w-k-e-w, I add p and w. At the second w, it's a duplicate, so I remove from the left: remove p, then remove the first w. Now I add the second w and continue. The window w-k-e gives length three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good. What about the complexity now?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each character is added and removed from the set at most once, so the total work is O of two-n, which simplifies to O of n. Space is O of n for the set. This is much better, but the left pointer sometimes moves multiple steps. Can we make it jump directly?

sections.title: Optimized Sliding Window with HashMap
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["String: 'p w w k e w'"] --> B["right=0: map={p:0}, left=0, max=1"]
    B --> C["right=1: map={p:0,w:1}, max=2"]
    C --> D["right=2: 'w' at 1 → left=2, map={p:0,w:2}"]
    D --> E["right=3: map={..,k:3}, max=2"]
    E --> F["right=4: map={..,e:4}, max=3"]
    F --> G["right=5: 'w' at 2 → left=3, map={..,w:5}"]
    G --> H["Result: 3 (window 'kew')"]
    style A fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style D fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style H fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: To avoid moving the left pointer one step at a time, I use a HashMap that stores each character's most recent index. When I encounter a duplicate, I jump the left pointer directly to one position after the previous occurrence of that character.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For p-w-w-k-e-w: at index two, w was last seen at index one. So left jumps to index two. At index five, w was last at index two, so left jumps to three. The window k-e-w has length three. At each step I update the max length.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The right pointer visits each character exactly once, so it's O of n time. Space is O of n for the HashMap, or O of one if we consider a fixed character set like ASCII. The key improvement is that the left pointer never backtracks through characters one by one.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    A["Brute Force\nO(n³) time"] -->|"Use sliding window"| B["HashSet Window\nO(n) time"]
    B -->|"Jump left pointer"| C["HashMap Window\nO(n) time"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice work. You moved from an O of n-cubed brute force to an O of n sliding window. The key insight was maintaining a window of unique characters and efficiently handling duplicates.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Yes. The brute force rechecks everything. The HashSet approach avoids that by sliding the window, and the HashMap goes further by jumping the left pointer directly. All three find the same answer, but the optimized version does the least redundant work.
